name: Neural Communication
summary: How neurons talk to each other through electrical and chemical signals.

sections.heading: The Action Potential
sections.content: Neurons communicate via action potentials — brief electrical pulses that travel along the axon at up to 120 m/s. This works through an all-or-nothing principle: when a neuron receives enough stimulation, voltage-gated sodium channels open in rapid succession down the axon, creating a wave of electrical depolarization. Myelin sheaths (produced by glial cells) insulate the axon and allow the signal to 'jump' between nodes of Ranvier, dramatically increasing speed — a process called saltatory conduction.

sections.heading: Synaptic Transmission
sections.content: When the action potential reaches the axon terminal, it triggers the release of neurotransmitters — chemical molecules that cross the synaptic cleft (a gap of about 20 nanometers) and bind to receptors on the next neuron.

sections.heading: Key Neurotransmitters
sections.content: Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, involved in learning and memory. GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, preventing over-excitation. Dopamine handles reward, motivation, and motor control; it is implicated in addiction and Parkinson's disease. Serotonin regulates mood, sleep, and appetite and is the target of most antidepressants. Acetylcholine is involved in memory, attention, and muscle activation and is lost in Alzheimer's disease.

sections.heading: Neural Circuits and Plasticity
sections.content: Individual synaptic connections are meaningless in isolation — it is the patterns of connectivity that matter. Neurons organize into circuits where the strength of connections can be modified by experience (synaptic plasticity). This is the biological basis of learning: 'neurons that fire together wire together' (Hebb's Rule).
